Before we pass from
public works in Nova Scotia, and a3 I may not have another opportunity, I desire to get some information from the minister as to Government telegraph lines. I understand that in Nova Scotia they are changing certain telegraph lines into telephone lines, and I have received letters indicating an anxiety on the part of the people to know whether the whole system in Cape Breton is to be turned into a telephone system. I desire also to bring to the attention of the minister what I regard as a very

serious matter in connection with the management of the telegraph lines. Last season I had occasion to be in the county of Victoria and to do more or less business with the telegraph lines. There is a telegraph system extending the whole length of the county, a distance of a hundred miles, with quite a number of offices. At certain seasons of the year that telegraph line is the <' nly means of communication of some places with the outside world, navigation being closed and there being no railways. On the occasion of the local election in Victoria county in February last, I was rather annoyed to find that the Government telegraph system had been converted into a machine for Tory politicians in that county. That whole system is entirely under the control of a man named *I * G. Dunlop, who is the superintendent. He went over that whole system and instructed the officers that he was authorized by the Minister of Public Works to authorize them to receive and send free all messages from representatives of the Conservative party during the time of the election. There was a swarm of these politicians all over that county and every one of them had free use of that line. Of course, those on the other side had no such privilege. For myself, any message that I [DOT]sent I paid for. I represented that county for years as a Government supporter, yet never sent a message without paying for *t as I did on any other line-I would not think of doing anything else. I submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that for this officer to take upon himself, without authority, I am sure, from the minister, to wire from his headquarters from Baddeck to the operators along that line instructing them to receive and send free messages presented to them by the agents of the Conservative party was an act which should earn his instant dismissal. I asked some of the operators the meaning of this thing and by what authority they sent these messages free. They answered that it was by the authority of the superintendent. And when I asked them om what authority the superintendent acted, they answered: We questioned him and he answered that it was on the authority of the minister. During the session I put a question on the Order Paper asking if there was any such authority and received the answer that there was not. So,
I bring to the notice of the committee, and particularly of the minister, the facts of the case and submit that such conduct cannot by any possibility be permitted. I have tMr. McKenzie.]
complete proof of the facts I allege. In fact, all the minister has to do is to ask his own officers if during the three weeks or so of that election campaign such instructions were not given by the superintendent. In view of the law laid down by no less an authority than the Prime Minister early in the career of the present Government that no officer should be permitted to take an offensive and unwarranted part in elections, I submit that while we fight our elections as vigorously as we can, it is altogether unfair that a Government system of communication should be placed at the disposal of one side absolutely free-and that the only system by which a telegram could be sent-while the other side can use it only by paying for it. Of course, paying for its use is altogether proper while the other is highly improper. What confidence can one have in a system of communication when we find the superintendent running the whole system in the interest of one side? What confidence can one have in sending a telegram over such a line? There is no secrecy about it-one might as well post his telegram on the side of the barn. I submit that abuses of this kind should be removed at once and steps taken to provide that they shall not occur again, no matter which party is in power.
I take the full responsibility for the truth of my statement of the facts. If the minister has any doubt about the matter, all he has to do is to inquire of any of his operators along the system from Baddeck to bay St. Lawrence, and he will find that what I am saying is true. I submit that an official who takes such a bold step as that without any authority from the department, should not hold his position for one day.

As regards the matter of changing the telegraph to a telephone system, I may say that, in response to a petition and request from the people 'in certain localities, certain changes have been made, and it is the object and purpose of the department to make those changes where they are deemed to be desirable and in the public interest. In regard to what my hon. friend has said in respect to the conduct of a certain officer of the department in connection with the telegraph'line, I may say at once that if this gentleman made the assertion that he had any authority from me so to use the telegraph line, he certainly stated what was absolutely untrue, for I certainly was not consulted in the matter; nor did I give

him 'permission to do what he did. The statement of my hon. friend is undoubtedly a serious one, and I will have the matter investigated at an early date with a view to ascertaining for myself what the facts are, and undertaking to deal with them as they should be dealt with.

I should like to know Jiow these telephone officials are appointed. Under ordinary conditions any person can get a telephone put in his house or in his office, but under the present Government system only a few persons have these telephone boxes. In my county offices have been established .in certain districts, and these offices have been placed in charge of staunch Tories; every other consideration seems to have been disregarded. I need not enumerate these officials; it will be readily understood that the purpose of the telephone system will be defeated if the minister continues to carry on that policy, which is absolutely contrary to the policy adopted and followed by any private telephone concern. If I happen to live along the line of this telephone .system, can I get a telephone if I apply to the Government for one?

If it were in the public interest and my hon. friend's application were justified, he would certainly have the same consideration as is given to any other citizen of the district. As I understand it, however, these boxes are simply pay stations, and are not for the use of individual citizens.
The minister gives me to understand, then, that any of the citizens in that district applying for a telephone will get one?
Oh, no.

Is it the minister's
intention to establish a telephone system similar to other telephone systems found all over the country? There is this difference between the telegraph system and the telephone system:	any one
can use the telephone, but only a skilled operator can use the telegraph. In my profession I would be glad to see a
number of people in various sections of the district have telephone boxes; they are willing to pay for them, and I can see no fairness in refusing these persons the privileges of the telephone system because they happen to be of one political persuasion rather than another.

It is not the purpose or the intention of the department to extend the telephone system beyond having it take the place of the telegraph system. In my judgment, the operation either of telegraph or of t"lenhone systems is a matter entirely for the provincial authorities. I for one would be prepared to recommend that the different telegraph systems should be taken over by the provinces. It is not our intention, however, to extend the telephone system to the use of individual persons.

I am sure the hon. minister will appreciate the absurdity of the position. When we had the telegraph, if I wanted to send a message to a friend twenty miles away, I could do so with some degree of secrecy, but now there is absolutely no secrecy, as our telephones are what they call the farm system, and everyone can listen to what is being said over the line. The minister can see clearly that to adopt such a system in substitution for a telegraph system is simply no good.
Does that not apply in the case of every telephone system in existence in the country?

Quite so, but if the hon. minister will extend the whole system to everybody who wants to take advantage of it, we will have some advantages with the disadvantages; as it is now, some of us have all the disadvantages and no advantage.

I cannot see that there is any particular disadvantage, but I can see that it would be impossible for us to extend the telephone system beyond having it take the place of the telegraph. We do not propose going into the telephone business.

The other telephone

I had a special purpose in asking as to the purpose of the minister to extend the operations of this telegraph line. They have a law in Nova Scotia under which, by some co-operation between the farmers and the Government, a cheap system of telephone lines is established throughout the country for the benefit of the farmers. I have a letter from a section of my county where the intention was to proceed under this local law to put in telephone lines and give the farmers the benefit of a telephone service, but some friends of the Government told them that there was no need to do that because the Government at Ottawa were going to put in a telephone system, and that there would be no need of duplicating the service in the county. We ought to have it distinctly understood as to whether the Government are going generally into the business of supplying telephones. If they are only going to put in a telephone where they had a telegraph office, that, of course, would only answer a certain purpose; Ibut if they intend to put in telephone connections generally along their lines wherever it is asked by any individual, of course there would be no sense in duplicating that same system by putting in a local system. The minister now says they are not going to do anything more than to put in a telephone wherever they have a telegraph office; that should be distinctly understood.
As I understand that is the length to which we propose to go.

When I was minister I took an appropriation for a small amount to purchase land at Hampton which would cost something under $1,000. My idea was to erect a building costing about $5,000. Hampton is a very small place, though very attractive. In view of the settled policy laid down by both sides of the House I did not feel justified in spending more than $5,000 for a building in a place so small as Hampton, which has not sufficient population to be incorporated. It has a population, I suppose, of about 150, and to spend $30,000 for a post-office in a village which certainly does not contain more than 200 is something which can hardly be justified. Hampton is the shire town of the county of Kings, which I formerly represented in the Legislature. There is a village called Hampton village a mile away, but it has a post-office of its own and consequently would not be served by this new building. I think my hon. friend ought to explain why this very large expenditure is being made, and which is so contrary to every declaration which was made in this House during the time I was Minister of Public Works. Member after member to my knowledge rose in his place and condemned the construction of a building costing $25,000 even in places with a population of 3,'000 or 4,000. It may be said I am responsible for this expenditure because I made provision to buy the land, but, as I have said, it never occurred to me to spend more than $5,000 on the building.

I think it is quite clear that when my hon. friend bought the land he was only trying to fool the people, and that he had no intention of spending any money whatever on a building. It is only another instance of how he made promises when he was in power but never fulfilled them. Hampton is the shire town of the
county of Kings, which is one of the most important counties in the province of New Brunswick. It has a population of more than five times what my hon. friend has stated at the least 1,000.

my hon. friend for Kings and Albert on his ability in getting such a large appropriation for his county, but I do not think the intelligent people of Hampton will appreciate this waste of public money. I think that the amount to be expended there is justified because, since the completion of the railway, Gaspe, or Gaspe Basin as it was formerly called, has become quite an important point, especially during the summer. Will he tell me where he is locating the new building and what amount he intends to spend. Will this be a building commensurate with other public buildings in the locality? Maisonneuve is a very progressive city. In fact, I think that, industrially speaking, after Montreal and Toronto, it is the first city in the Dominion.

speechtext: Ahead of Hamilton?
I am not certain of its position, but it certainly is one of the great industrial centres of the Dominion.

I had occasion to visit
Maisonneuve a short time ago and found a very prosperous condition indeed. They had erected there a public building that was a credit to the place, and the post-office site that had been selected would certainly have interfered with the view from the maginfi-cent building which the municipality of Maisonneuve had erected. We are simply

crossing the street and exchanging the property we had for a property directly opposite on Ontario street. We propose erecting a public building in keeping with the other public buildings being constructed at the present time.
Montreal-Postal station * A,' St. Janies street $30,000.
Is that a new building? And where is it?
This is the proposed new building on St. James street. It is what is known as the Carslake purchase.

You are not going to
do that for $30,000?
We may hear from it again in the Supplementaries.

With all due deference to my hon. friend, I think that this purchase of the Carslake site is not warranted. On the 27th of April last, I put some questions in this House which were answered by the Minister of Public Works, and which I quote from ' Hansard ':
Mr. Lemieux:
1.	Has the Government disposed of the property purchased a few years ago near Bona-venture station, St. James street, Montreal, for postal purposes?
2.	What is the superficial area of said property?
3.	What was the purchase price?
Mr. Rogers :
1.	No.
2.	15.732 feet.
3.	Taken in exchange, in 1907, for property on Cathedral street.
A few days afterwards the minister corrected the statement as regards the superficial area of the old property on St. James street, which Sir William Mulock bought when he was Postmaster General. The site purchased by Sir William Mulock is but a stone's throw from that which the Minister of Public Works contemplates purchasing- the Carslake hotel site. In his corrected statement the minister put the superficial area at something like ten or eleven thousand feet. I think that this area is quite sufficient to provide a building for the purpose proposed. I understand that this building is for the handling of the newspapers and parcel post. Now my hon. friend is going to invite much criticism if he does not exercise the greatest care in the purchase of the Carslake hotel property. First, it is not needed, as the Government already have one property, a property which it has held for years without using. In the second place it is known that a syndicate have secured the Carslake hotel for speculative

purposes. I do not know that the minister is aware of this, but as expropriation proceedings have toeen initiated, he will probably know very shortly that the price he will be asked before the valuation is made will be simply exorbitant. I predict that if the Government persist in obtaining that property from the speculators they will have to pay in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars for it. What are the facts? There is in Montreal a gentleman by the name of Harry A. Dorsey, who leased the present Carslake hotel from George T. O. Carslake. I have here the deed which was signed before Henry Fry, notary public for the province of Quebec, at Montreal on December 1, 1910. It is as follows:
Before Maltre Henry Fry, notary public, for the province of Quebec, residing and practising in the city of Montreal.
Harry A. Dorsey, of the city of Montreal, manager, hereto present and accepting, for, during and until the full end and term of five years and five months to be counted and reckoned on and from the first day of December, nineteen hundred and ten:
That certain building fronting on St. James Street, in the city of Montreal, near the corner of Windsor Street, and known as Carslake hotel, and being numbers 571, 573 and 575 St. James street with all the rights, members and appurtenances thereof, including the cost of electric fixtures, bar fixtures, counters, cigar counter, kitchen fixtures, range, heater, gas stove, sinks, racks, boilers, refrigerators, ice-box, fix tables, heating apparatus and cellar, pantry and other fixtures, which are considered as part of the property. The land included in this lease being lot number 725, on the official plan and book of reference of the St. Antoine ward, which fronts on St. James Street, the land immediately in the rear therof, being the southeast portion of lot number 726, on the said official plan and the southeast portion of lot No. 723 of said official plan ; the whole as shown edged in red and in green on a plan thereof made by Joseph Rielle, P.B.S., and of record in his office dated the fifth day of June, eighteen hundred and ninety-nine, and which property is that acquired by the lessor from the Royal Institution for the Advancement of Learning by deed of sale before Henry Fry, N.P., the third day of November, nineteen hundred and nine, etc.	.
The present lease is made for the sum of four thousand five hundred dollars ($4,500) per annum during the said term, which said lessee doth hereby promise and oblige himself to pay by even and equal consecutive quarterly payments of eleven hundred and twenty-five dollars ($1,125) each.
Then follow the ordinary clauses usually contained in such leases.
The lessee will have the right to buy property hereby leased at any time until the first day of May, nineteen hundred and sixteen, for the sum of ninety thousand dollars ($90,000) by giving to the lessor notice in writing of his
intention at least two months before the date on which he intends to purchase.
In the event of the premises being destroyed by fire in whole or in part, it is understood and agreed that the amount of the purchase price fixed by the present option shall be reduced by in amounts which the lessor may receive from the insurance company of the premises hereby leased and which is not expended in replacing damage caused by fire.
The lessor shall not be obliged to expend in repairs after the fire more than he received from the insurance, but the moneys so received are to be approved of by both parties.
The option to purchase hereby given shall be cancelled and ceased in case the lease itself is cancelled, provided always the lessee has a right to exercise the option to purchase within three months of the cancellation of this lease.
Whereof acted; at Montreal on the first day of December, nineteen hundred and ten, and of record in the office of the undersigned notary under number nine thousand six hundred and nine.
(Sgd.) Geo. Carslake.
Here is a property leased to Mr. Dorsey with an option to buy extending until the first day of May, 1916, for the sum of $90,000. This option and lease has been registered in the registry office at Montreal. I am certain that when the Government come to buy this property they will have to pay half a million dollars for it. This amount may startle my hon. friend, but I predict now that it will cost them that much. Is it worth while paying that amount when the Government already have the site which has been used for several years, which is still available and which is certainly sufficiently extensive for the needs of the public service? In Montreal it is common talk that this is a matter of speculation. Several real estate men in that city have written me since the matter became known to the public press declaring that the amount which is said to be about to be paid to the syndicate is certainly abnormal. If expropriation proceedings are going on, I would advise my hon. friend ro get as many real estate men as possible to establish the actual value of the property. I do not say that the property is not worth more than the $90,000 mentioned m the option to Mr. Dorsey, because property has increased in value since Mr. Dorsey leased the Carslake hotel, but there is a wide gap between $90,000 and $500,000, and I hope my hon. friend will see that the interests of the public are protected in this matter.

The committee may depend upon it that the greatest possible caie will be exercised in regard to thi3 matter.

For six ocr eight years the Post Office Department has been pressing for the erection of a building such as the one now proposed for the convenient handling of mail to and from the different stations in the city of Montreal. With that object in view, as far back as 1896, a site was purchased upon which to erect such a building and the Postmaster General of that day Sir William Mulock, purchased a large quantity of pneumatic tubing in order to convey the mails under ground to and from the Canadian Pacific and Grand Trunk stations'. For some reason or other, at the request of the Grand Trunk Railway Company the site at that time selected and purchased, which was apparently a very desirable site, and, if we had it to-day, would undoubtedly be the most desirable site for the purpose, was exchanged with the Grand Trunk Railway Company for the site t-o which my hon. friend refers as containing 15,000 square feet. Unfortunately the city of Montreal have established what they call a homologated line by which they take away from us about 4,500 feet of that particular property; and in doing so they leave the property in such an irregular state that it is entirely unsuited according to the officers of the Post Office Department, for a post office building at this particular point. That is the recommendation of Mr. Gaboury and the other officers of the Post Office Department.
As to the purchase of the Carslake hotel property, that has been done entirely on the recommendation of the officers of the Post Office Department who claim that it is the most desirable site for the purpose for which it is intended, desirable in that it is centrally located between the three stations in Montreal, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Northern railway; and it is proposed eventually that we shall adopt the system suggested and intended to be adopted by Sir William Mulock of transferring the mails underground to the three railway stations. We have on hand a very large quantity of pneumatic tubing purchased at that time ' by Sir William Mulock and still available for that purpose. In respect to the price of the CaTslake hotel property, every care will be exercised. We are not placing a valuation upon it but are simply leaving the value to be fixed by Judge Cassels of the Exchequer Court, and every care will be exercised and all evidence will be produced in order that the department and the Government may
[Mr. Roger- '
not be asked any more for the property than it is really worth. As to the option which my hon. friend has read, when this property was recommended by the officers of the Post Office Department we had no knowledge whatever as to who the owners were and it was only at a later date that they became known to us. We have had valuations made of the property by some of the leading real estate agents in the city of Montreal. The valuations range between $280,000 and $325,000. I can assure my hon. friend and the House that every precaution and every care will be taken that there will be no chance for anybody making any speculation or any money out of the country and out of the Government in respect of the purchase of tlhis property.
Montreal Postal station * G,' St. Lawrence division, $50,000.
That is at Prince Arthur and Elgin streets.

I think this vote is warranted; but I would call the attention of my hon. friend to the needs of the eastern section of St. Catherine street. From the papers of Montreal favourable to the Government it will be seen that there has been a general outcry in the eastern division of Montreal, say from Bleury street as far as Amherst, for more postal facilities. The large organs of public opinion have clamoured in vain during the last two or three years for better postal equipment on this street. For a number of years it has seemed as if St. Catherine street was becoming the real nerve centre of Montreal, and certainly the postal facilities are not sufficient in that district. I would ask my hon. friend, the next time he goes to Montreal, to make himself acquainted with that district and see that proper postal facilities are provided.

I have already promised to visit that district, because there is certainly a pressing necessity for a post office on St. Catherine street at some point between Maisonneuve and the post office we now have close to St. Catherine street on a side street. A post office will be erected there as soon as possible; but, of course, we cannot build all the post offices asked for in such a short time. I shall take the matter up as soon as I possibly can.
Murray Bay public building, $15,000.

Have you selected a site for the Murray Bay public building?

Murray Bay is like Gaspe Basin, it becomes really a town during three months in the summer, and the expenditure is justified, because there is a large revenue derived from these offices in summer.

The site is at Main Street and St. Antoine Street. The site is 60 by 100 feet, and the proposed -building is required for post office and customs purposes.
Quebec post office-enlargement and alterations, $250,000.
Is this extension to be on the front or the side of the building?

It is to make the building longer, but it will not interfere with the front.
Quebec-iso'ated cottages for contagious diseases and disinfecting building, etc., $18,000.
How many cottages are you building ?

It depends on the reports of the officers of the department.
Quebec-immigration building on Louise Embankment, $170,000.
Is that near completion ?
The building is already completed and occupied, but we are adding another story.
That will not cost $170,000.
That amount is to take care of another item as well. This extra story is required for the detention of those immigrants suffering from contagious diseases.

Before we leave the Quebec Estimates I would like to ask the minister whether he intends doing anything for Riviere du Loup public building. Some ornamental work is being done in connection with that building, and I would like to know if it is to be proceeded with. I do not see any item here. There is a small piece of land behind the building which would be very useful for a park for the citizens of the town. It would not cost very much and I would like to ask whether any item will be in the Supple-mentaries for that purpose ?
Something was done last year.

The work has not been completed. I would also ask the minister if he could put a tower and a clock on the
building. I think the citizens of the town have already sent in a petition to that effect.

Such a petition may have been sent in, but I have no recollection of it. If my hon. friend desires the information, I will obtain it for him. In regard to improving the grounds, I might say that we are doing some work there now and I will have the matter looked into.
In case the minister finds no petition in his department asking for a tower and a clock, I petition him myself to have them erected, and I think the Postmaster General will second me.
I am afraid I have no amount in the Estimates. If my hon. friend had made his request earlier, we would have taken it into consideration.
I thought the petition had been sent in and I expected there would be an item in the Supplementaries.

1 do not remember having received the petition.
Caledon public building, $1,500.
What is the population?
I have some knowledge of that country, but I do not know of such a place.

It would facilitate the
passing of these Estimates if the minister would give the population in each case.

The population is put
down here as 3,000, but that is evidently a mistake.
What county is it in?
Peel.
I have passed through the town and should say it has a population of 500 or 600, possibly 800. It is on the Owen Sound branch of the Canadian Pacific railway.

The minister
should instruct his officers not to refer to the census returns for information of this kind, because it has been proved time and again that they are incorrect and that a place mentioned in the Estimates and designated by the same name in the census returns do not comprise the same territory, the latter being much more extensive than the former.

My hon. friend may be quite right, but still the census returns can

be analysed to see whether a township has been added or anything of that kind. I think that it is the safest plan to consult the census returns. If you get away from that, you are bound to get into trouble.
The minister is sure there is such a place as Caledon?
There is a township called Caledon and a railway station called Caledon East, but I never heard of Caledon village.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken. It is quite a considerable village. I think the large brickyards that supply Toronto are near there.
The revenue of the post office is $476; money orders, $10,945; money orders paid, $4,300.
The item with reference to the Brantford public building might stand until the Ontario members are .'ere.

They can bring it up any time they like.
Georgetown public building, $20,000.
Will this be built of Georgetown or American stone?

I have asked the Minister of Public Works to build it of Georgetown stone without fail, and he has assured me that if the difference in cost, will not be too much he will do so. The Georgetown people are extremely anxious that this building should be built of stone, and if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) were up there himself he would second the proposition.
Can you satisfy the minister that it is good stone?
The chief architect is here, and he is able to tell you that no better stone can be found.
Are not the Georgetown people sufficiently patriotic to ensure that the price of the Georgetown stone will not be any more than the price of the imported stone?
If the Minister of Public Works will build it of Georgetown stone, the people of Georgetown will take no exception to that, you may be sure.

Speaking of these Militia buildings, I think the Minister of Public Works promised last year that .he would have them placed under a separate

heading, and not intermixed with what are public works expenditures proper. That is a good suggestion, and I think it ought to be arranged for next year.

The Minister of Militia
may have made the statement, but I have no recollection of having done so.
Do you think it would be a good thing?
I think it is the business of the Public Works Department to erect-all buildings.
Yes, but if we ask the Minister of Public Works to justify an expenditure on one drill hall or a militia building he cannot be expected to do so.

There may be something in the suggestion.
Milton public building, $20,000.
How much will this building cost before it is completed?
We are calling for tenders. The architect's estimate was $20,000; the population is 1,657.
Surely the building is going to cost more than $20,000?
I hope ,so.

If it did not cost more
than that the House would be astonished at the moderation of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson).

It does seem to me that in connection with expenditures on public buildings the present minister is responsible for departure from the established policy under the late Government. In many cases here we have been voting money for public buildings in towns of 100, 200, or 300 population. In my opinion the minister is embarking upon a very dangerous policy in that respect.
He has embarked on the steamer Dashaway.

If this is to be continued it will entail a much larger expenditure than the country is justified in making. The late Government, on the whole, confined public buildings to towns of 1,500 population and up, but there are scores of instances now of public buildings contemplated in places with a population of 500 and less.

I have said several times that while we acknowledge a few cases

where public buildings are being erected in places wheTe the population is not sufficient to warrant a large expenditure, in no case now do we adopt the idea of erecting a public building in a place unless it has
1,000	population.

You are voting here
money for the purchase of sites in towns where there is not one-quarter of a thousand population.
I. fear you are exaggerating.

No.

Are you going to add

outside of the cost of the foundation.

This- item is to make
provision for the complete remodelling of the fireproof throughout the old museum building on Sussex street to suit the requirements of the Department of Mines according to the following estimate submitted by the chief architect: Window enlarged for doorway and stairs, $829; covered boiler and pipe in basement, $722; contingencies, $449; total, $2,000.
What are you doing with that building now?

It is occupied by the
Mines Department.
Ottawa-new drill hall, $50,000.

What will become of
the drill hall at Cartier Square?

Nothing has been settled about the site of the new building yet. I suppose if we decide to buy a new site the present building will have to be sold.
Ottawa Parliament	buildings-improvements, $17,000.

What improvements
are to be considered?

This vote is to cover the cost of a new copper roof and skylight for the House of Commons and the Senate Chambers. The galvanized iron roof will no longer hold solder. This is also to cover other improvements which may be required during the fiscal year.

While repairing the elevators in the Langevin block, the minister might think also of the elevators in the House of Commons. I understand that recently my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) was caged in the elevator between this story and the next.
I got out again.

Almost every day the
elevator is stopped at great inconvenience



to members. One elevator, I think, is not sufficient for that section of the building, and there should foe another. And now I am to repeat my old request. The Government is spending large sums every year for public works in every part of the country, but it is neglecting, it seems to me, the interior of the Parliament buildings. This Parliament building is probably one of the noblest buildings in the world. As a massive and imposing pile, I think few public buildings can compare with it. But, while architecturally splendid on the outside, the interior is rather poor. This House of Commons is a very poor assembling place as compared with the House of Commons in South Africa and similar Chambers elsewhere. Our walls are bare, and there is nothing inspiring in the appearance of the place. Visit the Parliament buildings in England, and you find the walls covered with historical tableaux and the .halls crowded with the statues of the great. I think the Minister of Public Works would do well-and I believe he has still some ideals left, though he has been so long in Manitoba politics-[DOT] to think of giving this House an interior in keeping with the splendid exterior of the place. Why not have the history of the country written in paintings on our walls? We might have, for instance, a concourse of our distinguished painters to give us valuable representations of Canadian history. The library, too, is getting very crowded and is in a very poor state. You find the avenues blocked with newspaper files, blue-books and documents. I think the Minister of Public Works should see to it that the interior of out Parliament buildings is given more beauty.

I appreciate the force of my hon. friend's argument concerning the interior of these buildings. Certainly great improvements could be made. Yet I do not quite agree with him as to this Chamber being so much inferior to that of other countries. I confess that I think our Chamber is as good as the House of Commons in England. If we can get the time, we will give more careful consideration to the question of improvements here. One thing I might mention while on this point. It has been represented to me by several members that carpet on the floor of this Chamber is objectionable and this floor should be covered with the best linoleum we can procure. I would like to know the views of members on that subject. I think it would be desir-

able, before the assembling of the next Parliament, to try linoleum for a time. The present carpet is about worn out. Yet I would not like to make the change without consulting the members. As to improvements in the library, we have had a vote as the hon. member knows for a couple of years, but there have 'been so many things claiming attention that nothing has been done. But the vote is in for this year also, and I hope we shall 'be able to reach the matter.

Perhaps it is not quite fair to occupy the time of the committee at this late date discussing a matter of this kind, yet I cannot quite resist the temptation to say a word. It is unfair to complain of the Minister of Public Works, whoever he may be, about the condition of this building, and especially of this Chamber. That is a domestic matter that ought to engage the attention of members, and I assume that, as the minister has intimated, he will do nothing without consulting the members.
I notice that every Minister of Public Works promises consideration regarding the interior of the Chamber. My hon. friend has been here two or three years, and but little- time remains for him to distinguish himself in this Parliament. Either of two things may remove him from his position of influence: his departure for London, or, in the course of a very short time, his sitting on this side of the House. I think that there are two matters which ' should be considered seriously during the recess, and I would like to ask the minister to take them into consideration, and to submit some kind of proposal at the beginning of the next session. I have often thought that another floor or story might be added to this building in order to afford proper accommodation to the members. That, of course, is a question for the architect to decide; perhaps it could not be done, -but I think it is worth looking into. I have thought, too, that we need a new chamber -here, which could be supplied by building to the rear of the library, and by building a new library. I think these are matters to which we do not pay sufficient attention. It is quite true that the stay of any one of us in this House is very uncertain, but I think that we should take as deep an interest in this matter as if we were fully satisfied that we would -be here as representatives of the people for a great many years.

In reference to the serious portion of my hon. friend's remarks,

I realize that it is quite possible that the condition of the interior of the Parliament buildings has probably never received that careful consideration which it should receive, by reason of the fact that it is often difficult, on account of pressing business, to give to the matter the consideration which its importance requires. I would be entirely opposed to the placing of an extra story on this building, believing, as I do, that it would destroy its architectural beauty. As to the matter of a new chamber, there is some force in what my hon. friend says, but I would suggest that the most desirable location would be not where the library is, but on the west end. At any rate that is a matter well worthy of consideration. If I can possibly get the time during recess, 1 will endeavour to prepare some ideas to submit to Parliament when it assembles again with a view to bringing about improvements. If there is no objection from the members, I will undertake to see whether we can improve on this carpet in some way, as I think it is time it was removed.

Permit me to make a suggestion. I think that we would have to go a long way to find a room as beautiful as the library, but the whole effect is spoiled by the appearance of the ceiling. The practice of colouring summer kitchens indigo blue may have been in vogue forty years ago, but it certainly should not be permitted in that room. I would ask the minister to consider during the recess the advisability of having the whole dome ceiled with light oak or pine, in order to make it consonant with the beauty of the rest of the library. I do not think it would cost a great deal, and I am sure that we would all like to see the last of that indigo blue dome.

I do not agree with the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) in his comparison of this Chamber with that of the House of Commons in England. I was utterly astonished when I entered the House of Commons in London and the Chamber of the House of Lords. Ours is a palace compared with the Imperial House of Commons, in beauty, in size, and in any way you have a mind to take it; and we have nothing to be ashamed of in the House of Commons in Canada. I am sure that visitors who have seen both buildings can go away with but one opinion: as regards accommodation and in every other way, we have the superior Chamber of the two. Speaking of the 265$
library, two years ago a gentleman and his daughter whom I met on the way from Toronto came to Ottawa, and I took the opportunity of showing them through the buildings. Amongst other places, I showed them the library. The moment the door was opened, the girl exclaimed: ' Oh, this beats Washington,' and the father was obliged to say, ' hush '-he did not want anybody to hear it. I think we have in the library a beautiful structure of which we may well be proud. With regard to the carpet, in these times of falling revenue we can put up with the old carpet; I do-not think it is so bad after all. Let us make additions to some of our public buildings in the country; we need them more than we need a new carpet. At any rate, I do not approve of covering the floor with linoleum; I am afraid that that suggestion came from some manufacturer who has linoleum to sell. As to the enlargement of these buildings, I think that is a matter that Parliament should consider not at the end but at the beginning of a session, and I shall not attempt to discuss it at this stage.
Manitoba public buildings-Winnipeg drill hall, $300,000.	,

I notice that something is voted for every county in Manitoba except Provencher. That must be an oversight on the part of the minister. I have not raised any objection to any amount voted for any of these towns. I am glad to see them get the amounts and I think they are entitled to them; but at the same time I think that Provencher, which is the oldest county in Manitoba, should receive something. All I would ask is a post office for the town of Morris, not to exceed $10,000; perhaps it could be built for $7,000. The accommodation for the public in the present post office is sufficient for about six people. I hope that the minister will be able to provide for a new post office in the Supplementary Estimates, or else that he will provide for it next year.

My hon. friend is rather doing me an injustice in suggesting that 1 have not attempted to do anything for Provencher. We are providing in the Supplementary Estimates for a post office for Norwood, in my hon. friend's county, a growing and thriving town. I quite appreciate the suggestion that there is a reasonable necessity for a new post office in Morris, one of the oldest towns in the province and a very growing and prosperous place; and I can
I

assure my hon. friend that if I am not able to include it in the Supplementary Estimates, I shall make my recommendation and endeavour to include it in the Estimates for the next year.
Winnipeg'-railway postal station, $100,000.

I beg to move that this item he struck out. I might explain that Winnipeg requires a new postal station, and also a new immigration hall. The present immigration hall at Winnipeg has been condemned by the health authorities. Several of the rooms were dark, and it was impossible to get proper ventilation; for these and other reasons the building was condemned, and consequently some arrangement had to be made for a new building. It was found that the immigration building, when remodelled, would do very well for the postal station we require immediately adjoining the station, and we are therefore going to use the immigration building for that purpose. In the Supplementaries 'an item will he found providing for a new immigration hall. I therefore move that this item be dropped.

I have no criticism to offeT of the votes under the head of Saskatchewan except to the number, which I think is 'altogether too small. The minister knows very well that in point of population the province of Saskatchewan is the third province of this Dominion. I do not think I am speaking boastfully when I say that presently we expect Saskatchewan to be the great producing province of Canada, and as regards population, I think it will not be very long before it stands next to this great province of Ontario, and not very long after that before it is the leading province of Canada in point of population. I notice that the total amount appropriated for public buildings in Saskatchewan is less than a million dollars. Alberta, with a smaller population, is getting over $400,000 more than Saskatchewan, and British Columbia almost $1,000,000 more. The province of Manitoba, from which the minister comes, with a smaller population and a very much smaller area of settlement, has $300,000 more for public buildings than Saskatchewan. I think the committee has been very generous in the treatment accorded to all these votes in Ontario, especially in view of the fact that
I Mr. Rogers.]
the western provinces are fairly well represented on this side of the House to-night. In looking over the list of public buildings for Ontario, I notice that a great many small villages have items of considerable importance for drill halls, post offices, and so on. I would like a little better consideration to be given the province of Saskatchewan in the future Estimates of the Minister of Public Works. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent, I think the town of Humboldt is the only one where public money has been expended on a public building by the present Government, although I see the minister has an item of $20,000 for a public building at Wadena, Saskatchewan. Three great transcontinental railways run through my constituency: the Canadian Northern railway; south of that the Yorkton extension of the Canadian Pacific railway; and still further south the Grand Trunk Pacific. In view of the minister's generosity to all these little towns in Ontario, British Columbia and other provinces, I think that at least the divisional points on these three transcontinentals ought to have a little consideration. Take the Grand Trunk Pacific for instance. In Humboldt constituency Watrous is the divisional point and is widely known not only throughout the West, but throughout the East as a famous health resort due to its proximity to lake Manitou, the waters of which are supposed to have splendid medicinal qualities. Suiely a town of this importance with a population of 2,000 or thereabouts, ought to have at least one public building for a post office or something of that kind. The subland agency there might be accommodated in the same building. Another divisional point in my constituency is Wynyard, south of Quill lake, on the Canadian Pacific railway. Then there is also Lanigan, the junction point of the Pheasant Hills branch and the Yorkton branch of the Canadian Pacific railway. It is in a welhpopulated district and has a population of about 1,500. I recommend that the minister take into consideration the claims of at least the three points I have mentioned: Watrous, Lanigan and Wynyard. I do not think my criticism is at all unfair; in fact, I think it is eminently fair as I think the minister must recognize when he looks at the grand totals of the Estimates of the various provinces for public buildings. I hope the minister will take into consideration the three places I have mentioned. So far as the rest of the province is concerned, I think

hon. gentlemen should speak for their own constituencies.

I agree with my hon.
friend in this respect at all events, that the West is not getting any more than her share from the Parliament of Canada. So far as I am concerned, as a western man, I am always ready to lend a sympathetic ear to any legitimate expenditure in any of the growing towns in western Canada. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Neely) rather attempts, although I hope he did not intend it, to do me an injustice in comparing my attitude towards Saskatchewan with my attitude towards Alberta and Manitoba. I do not think, so far as I can remember, that any fair request has been made to me for the construction of a public building in any of the growing and thriving towns of Saskatchewan that is not recognized in the present Estimates, or which will not be provided for in the Supplementary Estimates. If this appropriation is smaller than my hon. friend thinks it should be, it certainly is not my fault, because if my hon. friend or any other hon. gentleman made a request for a public building and was able to show, as undoubtedly they could in certain cases, that a public building was in the interest of the people and was a necessity, I can assure him that it would have been recommended by me, and I would hope that it should be included in the Estimates. If my hon. friend will renew his request before the next Estimates are brought down, he will find that I will be ready to endeavour to secure the necessary sums for the erection of public buildings in the growing towns of Saskatchewan, in common with the other provinces of the West.

I am glad to hear the Minister of Public Works speak in this way. The members of this House have no opportunity of knowing what will be in the Estimates before they are brought down. I appreciate very much the attitude he assumes towards, the erection of public buildings in Saskatchewan, and I give him notice in advance, and I hope he will make a note of it, that from every point of view there should be public buildings erected in Watrous, on the Grand Trunk Pacific, and Wynyard and Lanigan on the Canadian Pacific railway.
Athabaska Landing-addition to public building, $5,000.

The building that has
been occupied there has been very inadequate; what sort of a public building is to be erected at Athabaska Landing?

I was just going to move that this item be amended by leaving out the words ' addition to public 9 p.m. building.' In view of the fact that the old building is so inadequate, the officers of the department recommended that a new building be erected at Athabaska Landing.

Will that building be
commenced this year?
Oh, yes.

What will be the total
cost?

I have not the architect's report yet, but it will be a building adequate to the requirements of the place. As my hon. friend knows the population there is not large at present, but it is the gateway to the great West beyond, and a building of reasonable proportions will be required.
I am not urging a large-expenditure, but I would like to know what particular branches of the public service will be accommodated in the old building and what branches in the new.
We will have a post office and a customs house, if required, in the new building.

What use will be mads
of the old building?
I do not know, but I am advised that it is not of much account.
Will the new building be on the site of the present building?

The people there are
petitioning for a different site.
Then it means the purchase of a new site and the erection of a new building.
Yes.
So that there will be two public buildings.

Yes.
Calgary-customs examining warehouse, $300.
Is Calgary a grow ing place?
Of course, it is. Has my hon. friend ever been in western Canada?

Yes.
[DOT]4202

Then he had better go
again and see the growth of Calgary.

Very much so.
I see there is a great disparity in the appropriations for the two towns.

Wait until you see the
Supplementaries.

Wait until you see us next year.
How far have the Calgary buildings progressed in construction?
The examining warehouse will be finished in August next.
Is the Canadian Northern into Calgary yet?

It is.

We are taking down the old building and erecting a new post office on the same site.
When will that be finished?
It will take all this summer to finish it and we have arranged for *quarters to take care of the business in the meantime.

I understand there is some dispute about the site of the drill hall at Calgary? There was a question of acquiring land in the park for some of these public buildings. Does the Government intend to acquire the land in the park or have they purchased a separate' site?

There was some difficulty about the site, but not so far as the Government is concerned; the difficulty was with the people of Calgary. Some wanted the site in the park and there was opposition to it. Edmonton post office-addition, $100,000.

What progress . is being
made with this addition ?

Chief Superintendent Ross of the Post Office Department reports as follows:

I would point out that I have been closely pressing on the attention of the department the necessity for additional floor space at Edmonton for some time past; and I would urge that consideration be given to the whole proposition, namely: either to acquire the lot immediately adjoining the Edmonton building and to erect thereon an addition to the present building for post office purposes, or to turn over to the post office the space on the upper floor of the Edmonton building.
When I was in Edmonton, on looking around I found rather at the back of the building, a piece of property on which the buildings were old and low, and which I thought would be a valuable piece of property for us to acquire in order to extend the post office. On the street the post office is on, and immediately adjoining it, there is a very large block which would make it difficult for us to extend the post office in that direction. Therefore I thought an extension at the back of the post office would be more desirable and the site easier to acquire.
Has the property been acquired, or what action has been taken ?

We sent the chief inspector, Mr. Ross, of Toronto, to report on the matter, and he agrees with my idea. The property has not yet been acquired.
Edmonton customs examining warehouse, $75,000.
Is that building under construction ?
Not yet.
Where is it to be erected ?
The site is on Peace avenue, 100 feet frontage by 150 feet deep.

Yes, for $63,000.
Has the contract been let ?

No.
Edmonton-new drill hall, $50,000.
What is the position in regard to this building?
The contract is let-
Has the property for this building been purchased or been provided by the city?
The city purchased the site from the Hudson Bay Company, and turned it over.

When is the .building to be completed?

Mr? ROGERS: Two years from the time the contract was let.

Last fall.
Grande Prairie immigration hall, 53,000.
What is the total cost of this immigration hall?
This item of $3,000 is to provide for the erection of the immigration hall. The appropriation in 1913-14 was $5,000. The expenditure was $2,000, requiring a revote of $3,000.
Is the building being constructed this summer, or when will it be constructed?
It will be put up this summer.

There is a new town being developed at Peace River crossing. A branch of the Dunvegan railroad has been chartered, and preparations have been made to carry it to Peace river crossing. That will be the first point at which the road will strike the navigation of the Peace river. There is a measurable boom in progress there now. There is no question about it being a permanent point, and I would like to take this opportunity of bringing it to the attention of the minister with a view to consideration in the future, although there has been nothing there until the last month or two. Owing to the fixity of that point as a railroad point, there has been a very strong direction of public attention and occupation to it; and I think the minister will be acting in the public interest, if, when preparing his next Estimates, he will take into consideration the requirements of this particular point.

We shall be glad to take notice of my hon. friend's recommendation and endeavour to meet his wishes in the matter.
Red Deer public building, $35,000.

May we have an assurance from the Minister of Public Works that this vote of $35,000 is not intended to seduce the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) away from the paths of economic and mental rectitude, or is the building actually required?

If I thought a monetary consideration would induce my hon. friend from Red Deer to depart from his economic ideas, it would not be an item of $35,000
that I would place here, but perhaps $35,000,000.
Vegreville public building, $30,000.

Is this building under
construction?
No, the contract has not yet been let.
Has the property been purchased?

Yes, we have the site.
Vermilion public building-$20,000.
What is the position in regard to the proposed Vermilion public building?

We have got the site, but no contract has yet been let. Both the VegTeville public building and the Vermilion public building will be gone on with this summer.
Duncan's Station public building, $40,000.
Mr. A. K. MAjCLEAN : How big a place is Duncan's Station?

I may tell the hon. member that the building is completed and occupied. The population of the place is about 2,000, tout there is a very large contributory country. The building is built and the janitor appointed.
Mr. MAC-LEAN: Then, what is this $40,000 'for? Surely the contractor would not 'be waiting all this time for $40,000 if the building were completed.
There is a re-vote here of $20,000. Th-e contract was $37,000, and it was let on the 12th of August, 1913. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Shepherd) is mistaken about the building being completed.
Perhaps it has not been commenced yet.
Yes, it has.

Is there any doubt about that? Perhaps the janitor was appointed before the building was commenced?
Mr. -SHEPHERD: I know I have had an application to appoint a janitor.
Oh, oh.
Only one?
Only one; I may say that the building is not yet completed; it lacks the clock.
When was it completed?
I tell the hon. member it is not yet completed; it lacks the clock.
When was it completed minus the clock?
Very recently.
Within twelve months?
Yes, I think so.
Was the hon. member ever in this' building?
Does the hon. gentleman wish it to be inferred that I am a stranger in Duncan?

I could infer a great
deal. I am almost afraid he is a stranger in Duncan, though that seems hardly possible. Yet I am inclined to think that he is mistaken about this building being completed. If he is sure about it and is not a stranger in Duncan he can tell me when it was completed. Was it a year ago-two years ago-three years ago?

If the hon. gentleman will read the Estimates he will surely not gain the idea that it was two or three years ago. I can assure the hon. member the building is fairly complete within the last year. Is that the information he wants to get?
It is not very definite. Can he tell me, was the building completed in July or August of last year?

I hardly know what the hon. gentleman wishes me to tell him. But I might remind him that I have been here about six months and the building was completed before I came here in January. Does that satisfy him?
No, it does not. Perhaps the minister can tell me-am I correct in assuming that the building is not commenced yet?
Yes, it has been commenced.
I suppose nothing substantial has been done, seeing that $40,000 is wanted.
The time for completion is fixed in 1915.
Well, the building is not finished. Or is it finished. I want to know what this $40,000 is for. Strike it out if it is not wanted.
If the building is not finished, why has the janitor been appointed?

Nobody said he was appointed, but only that an application had been received.
Prince Rupert drill hall, $35,000.
Perhaps some one can tell us the present population of Prince Rupert. I understand it is a comparatively new place.
It is growing very rapidly. The census of 1911 gives it a population of 4,771. It is the terminus of a transcontinental line and will undoubtedly grow.
I have been told that the population of Prince Rupert is less than it was when the census was taken.
Oh, no.

The minister invited
inquiry regarding military matters. Will he please tell us when the regiment was established for which this drill hall is intended and what is the strength of it? How long is it since they started military operations in that part of the country?

A free site has been donated and deeded to the department by the corporation of Prince Rupert. This site is located on Borden street and extends through Summit Avenue. Prince Rupert is under military district No. 11, headquarters of Earl Grey's Own Rifles, one company, Captain A. D. Stork. The following particulars are given by the Department of Militia and Defence, February 15, 1913:
Re Prince Rupert drill hall. There is at present no drill hall or armoury accommodation for the company of Earl Grey's Own Rifles stationed here. As the place is growing rapidly it is altogether likely that other units will be raised in the near future. It is understood that a suitable site will he provided.
Do they go to camp there and drill year after year?

They will have annua]
drill as do the volunteers in other parts of Canada.
Is that a guess on the part of the minister, or does he know?

In common with other
regiments of volunteers, they will go out during a certain period Of the year for annual camp and drill.

That is a matter of reasoning. Does the hon. minister know

anything about the camp strength of the regiment?

I have no report as to
that.

This is but another of the fanciful ideas of the Minister of Militia designed for .the purpose of throwing away $35,000 on something that is not required at all. Many other works are required in this country on which this money could, properly be expended. I do not wish to put the responsibility of these expenditures on the Minister of Public Works, as he inherits them in an indirect way, but he is stepping into the breach and must take the responsibility for these extravagant expenditures which have not the slightest conceivable justification.
Vancouver public buildings-improvements, renewals, repairs, etc., $5,000.

There is a general vote under item 5 for Dominion public buildings, and one would naturally assume that this would include general repairs to public buildings in the province in question. Should that not be sufficient for the whole province?

It has been the practice of the department to have a vote for the public buildings in the cities; this $5,000 is to meet the requirements for repairs, and so on, to public buildings outside the principal cities.
Victoria-new drill hall, $150,000.
Why is this new drill necessary? Is the old one insufficient to accommodate the militia at Victoria?
I have not before me information with respect to this, but I shall be glad to let the item stand until we get the information.

I think that would be better. I was quite serious the other night when I told the minister that the Minister of Militia and Defence, who is responsible for these things, should be here to see them through the House. The expenditure of such a large amount of money as this is a serious matter, and we should have some satisfactory explanation with regard to it.
Item stands.
William's Head quarantine station-new buildings, improvements and repairs to existing buildings, fittings, etc., $75,000.
Where is William's Head?
Near Victoria.
That is the quarantine station for Victoria?
All incoming vessels clear there.
The expenditure for improvements to the Victoria post office seems to be very large. What are they going to do to the post office?

That is a very extensive and a very necessary work. They are sorting the mails outside.

Are you going to install burglar alarms in the Public Works Department?

This is for the receiver general's offices in the different provinces.
Ottawa public buildings-elevator attendants, $50,000.

I understand that the elevator men in the buildings here have had their wages cut during the present session, and that on Sundays they do not get the same rate as they used to receive. I think that when public servants are required to work on Sundays they should get half as much again as they get on ordinary working days. Our public servants in this- country as a rule receive too little pay as it is. When you require an elevator man to work here for twelve hours on Sunday, when the rest of the people of the country are supposed to be resting and going to church and praying, and that sort of thing, these men should at least receive one-half more than they do for an ordinary day.
There has not been a reduction in the salaries.
Are they not working longer hours ?

They are getting extra pay for their Sunday work. Nothing has been brought to my attention in connection with the matter.
Ottawa public buildings-heating, including salaries of engineers, firemen and watchmen, $175,000.
I understand that the department have installed a new heating apparatus called the Presto heater.

Certain changes have been made in some of the furnaces to increase the draft, and two Presto heaters have been installed in the Langevin block. The chief

architect informs me that they are working very well.
What is the cost ?

$1,600 apiece.
Dominion public buildings-rents, $600,000.
What is the reason ' for the great increase in rent, from $375,001 to $600,000 ?
The service is growing and we require more space all the time.
Not at that rate, though.
Pretty nearly. That includes items for the various provinces.
Is it the practice of the department to accept tenders for coal for Government buildings that are not the lowest tenders ?
It is always the practice under ordinary circumstances to accept the lowest tender in everything.
What would be the cause for not doing so ?
It would be some extraordinary cause, perhaps a coal strike.

I have papers here in answer to an Order of the House in connection with the supply of coal for the public building at Lunenburg. Tenders were asked last year for that building, and one John B. Young was advised that his tender was the lowest, and the caretaker of the public building was advised to so instruct Mr. Young. I am sure I did not get all the papers, because I know that some correspondence passsed with the department which is not upon the file. Mr. Young was advised by the architect in charge of maintenance that his tender was accepted. There was a hiatus after that and nothing could be learned as to what was going on or what was to be done by the Department of Public Works. A little later it transpired that the contract had been awarded to another party who had tendered at the same time as Mr. Young. If, as the department said, Mr. Young's tender was the lowest, it is a very serious matter to have the contract awarded to another party. I would like to hear w>>
at the minister has to say about it.

If such is the case I have no knowledge of it. My hon. friend will understand that it is impossible for me to keep in mind the details of a multitude of contracts. I have no recollection of ever

awarding a contract to other than the lowest tenderer. I think there must be some mistake about my hon. friend's statement that he did not receive all the information that is on the files in the department. Since I have been in charge of the Public Works Department I do not believe a return has ever been brought down that did not embody all the information asked for that was on record in the department.

On August 2, 1913, the caretaker of this building was advised that the contract had been awarded to Mr. Young, but on August 9 that letter was cancelled by a telegram to the caretaker, as follows:
Cancel letter of second instant re coal contract. Contract not yet awarded.
Who signed that letter?

P. Shearson
Gregory. I have not the slightest doubt in the world myself Mr. Young's tender was the lowest and that the Government awarded the contract to him, but something has since occurred which I think is hardly creditable to the department. Of course I do not expect the minister to carry all the facts in a matter of this kind in his head, but if possible I would like the minister to look into this matter and write me.

I will.
Water, $39,000.

There is no reason why I should bring this matter to the attention of the minister any more than any other member, but those of us who are obliged to keep house in Ottawa find it an extraordinary thing that we cannot have pure water without going into the highways and byways and buying it. This water question has been a disgrace to the city of Ottawa for the last ten years. I have frequently brought it to the attention of other ministers of Public Works as well as the present minister. Surely something can be done to remove this difficulty. I asked the late Minister of Public Works, Hon. F. D. Monk, to stop paying for any water until we got a proper supply. In any other line of trade, whether it is Ibutlter, beef, potatoes, or anything else, you must sell a merchantable article before you can expect to be paid; but it seems to be different with water. The city of Ottawa is selling water to those of us who come here for a short time and to the residents, but we cannot use it. We have to go out in the streets

to 'buy water, otherwise we are in danger of pestilence breaking out in our families. At the same time we are compelled to pay for this undrinkable water, and the Government are paying hundreds of thousands of dollars every year for water that is not fit to be used at all. Strong language could be used in connection' with this water question and in connection with the civic government of Ottawa, but that is no good, and I am not going to do it. There is only one way to protect ourselves, and that is through bringing the influence of the Government and the Department of Public Works to bear upon the subject. The minister knows what it means to live in a city where you do not feel safe in drinking the water. Every member of the House and every man in the city knows what it is just as well as I do, and surely something should be done to help along whatever proper steps are being taken by the city to remove this difficulty, and the tax- although that is a comparatively small matter-but, most of all, the enormous inconvenience that is caused to people coming here by having to go outside to get their drinking water, because the water connected with the House is not fit to use; and, even then, they do not know' what they are getting. I hope the minister will use the large influence of his department in trying to bring about a better state of affairs in regard to Ottawa's water question.

My hon. friend can quite understand that it would be difficult for me to undertake to regulate the civic government of Ottawa. At the same time I am bound to acknowledge that I personally very largely share tire views of my hon. friend as regards the water supply of Ottawa. I might say that the water supplied in the House of Commons and in all the public buildings is absolutely pure and absolutely safe. lit is all sterilized, boiled or filtered, and is as pure as it is possible to make water. We have it tested regularly and invariably the tests show that the water is entirely pure 'and therefore safe. Ini regard to outside conditions, if it were possible for me by any means at my command to remedy conditions in Ottawa, I would be veTy glad to do so. I shall not lose sight of any such opportunity.	i

Is the ice used in
the public buildings taken from the Ottawa river?	[DOT]

It is artificial ice mechanically made.
Nova Scotia-harbours and rivers, $889,550.

I have a few words
to address to the Minister of Public Works in connection with the harbour at Glace Ray which is the distributing point for foodstuffs for a population of some 35,000 or
40,000	people. The railway facilities at Glace Bay are not good. The terminus of the Intercolonial railway is at Sydney, and the residents of Giace Ray and the surrounding country have to pay a double freight rate upon their food-stuffs. The harbour at Glace Bay is perhaps not a public harbour, but a former government spent money in extending the breakwater .there and dredging the harbour. They recognized that it was a harbour for the public benefit. Glace Bay used to be the shipping port of the Dominion Coal Company and other companies operating in that section, but now they use Louisburg and Sydney and have given up looking after Glace Bay harbour. In the last two or three years the harbour has filled np, and last year it was almost impossible for the ships from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick to enter it owing to its being filled up with sand. I would like to ask the minister if he can do something towards improving that harbour. I know all the Pa-inee Edward Island members take a deep interest in this matter. It would take very little money to improve the harbour. The Government steamer Canada formerly used to come in there, but a ship of half that size cannot get in now. I hope it will not be said that this is not a public harbour, because the late Government recognized it as such, and spent money in di edging and in extending the wharf. It is a serious matter for the thirty-five thousand people in the vicinity that they cannot get their produce other than by hauling it over two railways at a large increase of cost. I hope the minister will see that the entrance to the harbour is dTedged this year.

In going over the dredging programme for the coming year, we have already made arrangements to do a certain amount of work to meet the requirements at Glace Bay. I am afraid it will be impossible to do anything on the wharf this year, but we will endeavour to look after the dredging.

Baddeck-repairs to wharf, $550.
W'hat is the matter with this wharf; dt is comparatively new?
The amount is requested by the district engineer to renew the covering of some of the stringers and beams in the wharf which are in a -bad condition from wear and decay.

I am told that the
wharfinger now attempts to collect dues on this wharf while formerly there were none charged. A large traffic for the Intercolonial railway comes over the wharfs at Iona and Baddeck, and I have always contended that they are essential to the Government railways, and that therefore no charge should be made to individuals using them. The same observation would apply to the public wharfs in Victoria county, many of which are breakwaters built to afford shelter to the boats of the fishermen. If, as I understand, an attempt is made to charge the fishermen who take their boats to these wharfs, and spread their nets, I must enter a most vigorous protest against any such proceeding. It was never the intention of the Government to charge the fishermen any dues.

I have not the information my hon. friend asks, but if he will come to the department any day or drop me a line I will see that the information he requires is given to him as soon as possible.

Cow bay?

I have not that information at hand, but evidently
10 p.m. there has been a large expenditure from time to time on this wharf, as up to the 31st of March, 1913, it represented $300,000.

I shall be glad to get

Has the minister had
any application on behalf of the Broughton Coal, Iron and Railway Company for a wharf at Round island, where the company is establishing a terminus of their road as a shipping point?

strongly pressed as to that and I think my
